title: The Power Progression
hook: Prototype arms, delivery reports, and old renewal notes each ask for a different kind of power.
counterintuition: Counterintuitively, the power you want may be unavailable because the business is too early, too late, or in the wrong window to build it.
tryThisNow: Choose origination, take-off, or stability for your project. Then name the one power that the current stage can still build.
keyTakeaway: The power progression matches powers to timing: origination favors counter-positioning and cornered resources, take-off favors scale, networks, and switching costs, and stability favors process and brand.

breakdown.fastRead:
Prototype arms hang motionless above Grace's table of colored planning cards. She moves the brand campaign out of the origination column and places the exclusive actuator option there instead. The company does not yet have enough market history for brand power. It may still have time to corner a resource.

The progression is a timing discipline: some powers are built before the market is obvious, some only after demand begins to run. Wanting a power is not the same as being in the window where that power can form.
breakdown.deepRead:
Grace sorts the cards by stage, not by preference. Origination is the early search, when counter-positioning or cornered resource may be possible because the market is still taking shape. Take-off is when demand begins to run and scale economies, network economies, or switching costs can widen. Stability is when process power or branding may become plausible because the business has repeated activity, trust, and time.

The sequence is not a law of nature. It is a warning about windows.

Luca sees take-off at a meal-kit company. Delivery density, recipe data, and saved preferences are no longer isolated reports. They are the powers that can form as local retention improves: scale in denser routes, switching costs in saved preferences, data that may improve recommendations.

Timing matters because some moves expire. A late cornered resource may no longer matter after standards and substitutes settle. A brand campaign before product-market proof may spend money before there is history to believe.

The stage narrows the useful question.

A stage is not a trophy. It is a constraint on what evidence can mean. The same initiative can be wise in take-off and wasteful in stability, or premature in origination and urgent six months later.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 9:03 a.m., Luca spreads three reports across the packing table: delivery density, recipe data, and saved preferences. Six months ago, the company was still proving that families would reorder. Now local retention is strong, and the reports point toward take-off powers. Denser routes can lower cost. Saved preferences can create switching costs. Recipe data can make the next week easier to buy.

This is not a deterministic life cycle. A company does not earn a power just because it ages. Stage fit only tells you which powers are plausible enough to investigate. A young firm can waste money pretending to have brand. A stable firm can waste attention chasing a counter-positioning move that would have been available only before the old model hardened.

Which window is actually open right now?

Marta answers from the other end. Her industrial-sensor firm has years of installation tickets, renewal notes, and a service playbook. The early fight is over. In the postmortem, she marks which stability power is real and which is nostalgia. Process power might sit in the service routines. Branding might sit in years of trusted installations. A fresh counter-positioning story would be theater unless the old model has a new self-harm trap.

The supported sequence is straightforward. Counter-positioning and cornered resource often fit origination because invention and access choices happen before the market is obvious. Scale economies, network economies, and switching costs often fit take-off because demand, users, and accumulated setup begin to compound. Process power and branding often fit stability because systems and trust require repeated performance over time.

Adaeze uses the progression in a surplus lab-equipment marketplace. She asks the team to predict the week when one more seller helps existing buyers, then compares the guess with the listing log. Before that week, seeding is an origination problem. After that week, network economies become a live take-off question. The same marketplace needs different power questions at different moments.

Timing also closes doors. Ryan places a patent filing date beside a substitute catalog and a standards sheet for craft tools. The patent might have mattered before the market standardized around a different part. Filed late, it may protect a feature nobody needs. The right power arriving after the window can become an expensive souvenir.

Javier makes the review practical. He puts a quarterly initiative list under origination, take-off, and stability labels, then crosses out the funding line for an initiative whose window has passed. The room gets quiet because the move is not bad in the abstract. It is mistimed.

The progression does not remove judgment. It disciplines desire. Ask where the business is, which powers that stage can still build, and which tempting powers now belong to the past or the future. A strong strategy respects the clock.

examples.title: Grace moves the brand card

planSpec.domain: robotics startup reviewing whether to chase brand before product-market proof
planSpec.audience: founder matching power pursuit to origination
planSpec.stakes: branding is premature if the firm still needs a cornered technical resource or counter-positioned model
planSpec.requiredBeat: Grace moves the brand campaign card out of the origination column and puts the exclusive actuator option where the first power can form.

examples.scenario: At 7:55 p.m. in a robotics workshop, Grace stands over prototype arms hanging motionless above a table of colored planning cards. She has three stage columns marked origination, take-off, and stability. The brand campaign card looks exciting, but the customer proof is thin. She moves it out of origination and places the exclusive actuator option there instead. She must decide whether to chase a future brand or build the resource that can matter now.
examples.whatToDo: Sort each power by stage before funding it. In origination, test counter-positioning or cornered-resource paths before spending on brand signals the market has not learned to trust.
examples.whyItMatters: Branding needs history, while early access or business-model choices may still be available. The wrong stage turns a good power into a premature expense.

examples.title: Luca sorts the take-off reports

planSpec.domain: meal-kit company entering take-off after local retention improves
planSpec.audience: operator deciding whether scale, network, or switching costs can now emerge
planSpec.stakes: the window has shifted from inventing the model to using volume and retention before rivals crowd in
planSpec.requiredBeat: Luca sorts delivery density, recipe data, and saved preferences into the take-off powers that are actually forming.

examples.scenario: At 9:03 a.m., Luca spreads three reports across the packing table: delivery density, recipe data, and saved preferences. Local retention has improved for eight straight weeks. He sorts the reports under scale economies, network effects, and switching costs, then pushes the old product-discovery notes aside. The company is no longer asking if families will reorder; it is deciding which take-off power can grow before rivals crowd in.
examples.whatToDo: Use the take-off evidence in front of you. Test route density, user data, and saved preferences for scale, network, or switching-cost potential while demand is running.
examples.whyItMatters: Take-off is the window where volume and repeated use can harden into power. Treating it like origination wastes the data and demand that just became useful.

examples.title: Marta separates power from nostalgia

planSpec.domain: industrial-sensor firm reaching stability after years of installations
planSpec.audience: strategy lead checking whether process power or brand now fits better than counter-positioning
planSpec.stakes: late-stage advantage should come from embedded installation routines or trust, not a belated entrant move
planSpec.requiredBeat: Marta reviews old install tickets and customer renewal notes, then marks which stability power is real and which is nostalgia.

examples.scenario: It took Marta five renewals to see that the early fight was over. In the postmortem, she opens old install tickets, renewal notes, and the service playbook from three years of industrial-sensor work. The sales team wants a fresh entrant story. Marta marks the stability powers instead: process routines that reduce failures and trust that helps renewals. She also marks the counter-positioning idea as nostalgia.
examples.whatToDo: Use stability evidence: repeated routines, service history, and renewal trust. Do not revive an early-stage story unless the old incumbent trap truly exists again.
examples.whyItMatters: Later-stage firms often have the raw material for process or brand power. Chasing an origination move after the window closes can distract from powers that time has made possible.

examples.title: Adaeze predicts the useful seller

planSpec.domain: new marketplace for surplus laboratory equipment choosing when to seed buyers and sellers
planSpec.audience: product lead tracking the transition from origination to take-off
planSpec.stakes: the marketplace cannot claim network power until enough qualified users make the product better for each other
planSpec.requiredBeat: Adaeze asks the team to predict the first week when an added seller helps existing buyers, then compares it with the actual listing log.

examples.scenario: "Which week does one more seller help someone already here?" Adaeze asks in a university lab-equipment marketplace office at 10:20 a.m., pointing to a seller seed list and a buyer request sheet. The team predicts week six. She opens the listing log and shows the first week when added microscopes matched existing buyer alerts. Before the next seed budget is approved, she must decide if the marketplace is still in origination or entering a take-off network window.
examples.whatToDo: Find the first week when added sellers improve matches for existing buyers. Keep seeding until that point, then manage the marketplace as a take-off network question.
examples.whyItMatters: Network power is mistimed before users help one another. The stage changes when the product begins compounding through participant value, not when the team wants it to.

examples.title: Ryan dates the late patent

planSpec.domain: craft-tool manufacturer deciding whether a late patent can still corner a resource
planSpec.audience: reader evaluating timing pressure after the market has stabilized
planSpec.stakes: a resource that could have mattered in origination may be too late once substitutes and standards are fixed
planSpec.requiredBeat: Ryan places the patent filing date against the substitute catalog and decides whether the window has already closed.

examples.scenario: At 4:05 p.m. in a craft-tool parts office, Ryan asks what happens when the right power arrives after the market stops needing it. He places the patent filing date beside a substitute catalog and the standards sheet. The protected feature would have mattered two years ago. Now buyers have standardized around a cheaper insert. Before paying maintenance fees, Ryan must decide whether the patent still corners a resource or only records a missed window.
examples.whatToDo: Compare the filing date with standards and substitutes. Treat the patent as live only if the protected resource still changes value and rivals cannot route around it.
examples.whyItMatters: Timing can drain a resource of strategic force. A power that fit origination may matter little after substitutes and standards settle.

examples.title: Javier crosses out the late line

planSpec.domain: regional payments firm conducting a quarterly power review
planSpec.audience: executive team deciding which power is emerging, fading, or unavailable
planSpec.stakes: bad timing wastes investment on a power that belongs to a stage the firm has already passed
planSpec.requiredBeat: Javier has you place each initiative under origination, take-off, or stability, then cross out the ones whose window has passed.

examples.scenario: In a Madrid boardroom at 6:30 p.m., Javier feels the room quiet when the old initiative lands under the wrong stage. He places the quarterly initiative list below origination, take-off, and stability labels. Before the review, every line had a sponsor. After the stage sort, he crosses out the funding line for a late cornered-resource bet and moves the service-playbook investment under stability. The team now has to fund timing, not nostalgia.
examples.whatToDo: Run each initiative through the stage labels and cross out the ones whose window has passed. Move resources toward powers the current stage can still build.
examples.whyItMatters: A good idea can be strategically dead if the timing is wrong. The progression prevents teams from funding yesterday's opening with today's budget.

questions.prompt: A pre-revenue robotics startup wants to spend heavily on brand advertising before customers understand the product. It also has a chance to secure exclusive access to a key actuator. Which stage logic applies?
choices: Origination often favors access or model choices before brand history exists
Stability powers always come first
Branding is easiest before anyone has used the product
questions.explanation: In origination, cornered resource or counter-positioning may be live while brand history is thin. Stability powers need repeated performance and trust, which the startup lacks.

questions.prompt: A meal-kit company has strong local retention and enough order volume to improve routes and saved preferences. Which powers become especially worth testing?
choices: Only branding, because customers have heard of it
Scale economies, network economies, and switching costs in the take-off window
Only counter-positioning, because every firm is always early
questions.explanation: Take-off is when demand and repeated use can support scale, networks, or switching costs. Brand may come later, and counter-positioning is not automatically live at every stage.

questions.prompt: An industrial-sensor firm has years of install tickets, service routines, and renewal trust. A manager wants to revive an early entrant story instead. What should the team examine first?
choices: Whether the firm can pretend it is still new
Whether all old tickets should be deleted
Whether stability has created process or brand power from repeated performance
questions.explanation: Stability gives raw material for process power and branding. Acting new may be theater if the early window has passed. The old records are evidence, not clutter.

questions.prompt: A marketplace team wants to claim network effects before any added seller improves matches for existing buyers. What should the product lead do?
choices: Claim the network now because marketplaces always have network effects
Keep seeding and wait for evidence that participants improve value for one another
Switch immediately to brand advertising
questions.explanation: Network power is live only when added participants help existing participants. Before that, the marketplace may still be in origination or seeding mode.

questions.prompt: A patent would have blocked rivals in an early market, but standards have since settled around a substitute. What does the progression lens reveal?
choices: Every patent remains a cornered resource forever
The firm should pursue network power instead because patents are late
The patent may have missed its timing window
questions.explanation: Timing can narrow later options. A resource that mattered before standards settled may lose force after substitutes become normal. The answer is not to assume a different power without evidence.

questions.prompt: A stable consumer brand wants to build process power in a production system it has refined for years. Why might that stage fit better than origination?
choices: Process power often needs repeated activity and embedded routines over time
Process power requires no history at all
Origination is the only time any power can form
questions.explanation: Process power usually depends on interlocking activities that mature through repeated performance. Origination may create other powers, but it is not the only stage where power can form.

questions.prompt: A payments firm funds a late resource-cornering project even though substitutes are standard and its best evidence now sits in service routines and customer trust. What should a quarterly review recommend?
choices: Keep funding the late resource bet because sunk effort proves commitment
Reallocate toward powers the current stability stage can still build
Stop strategy work because every window has closed
questions.explanation: The review should respect timing. If the resource window closed, service routines and trust may support process or brand power. Sunk effort is not stage fit.

questions.prompt: A founder says, "We will choose branding, network effects, and process power this year because those sound strongest." What is the best critique?
choices: Choosing many powers always guarantees one will work
The strongest powers are always branding and process
Power choice must reflect stage and evidence, not preference
questions.explanation: The progression disciplines desire. A firm should ask which powers its stage and evidence can support. Listing attractive powers is not the same as building them.

questions.prompt: A young company has a business model incumbents cannot copy without harming their current revenue. Demand is still uncertain, and there is little scale. Which power fits the stage best?
choices: Counter-positioning in origination, if the model is superior and painful to copy
Process power in stability, because all startups have mature processes
Branding, because uncertain demand always creates trust
questions.explanation: Origination can fit counter-positioning when invention creates an incumbent trap. Scale and process are not supported by the evidence, and uncertain demand does not create brand trust by itself.

reviewCards.front: What three stages should you retrieve when timing a power?
reviewCards.back: Origination, take-off, and stability. Each stage makes different powers more plausible and makes other powers premature or late.
Counter-positioning and cornered resource, because early invention and access choices can form before the market is obvious.
Scale economies, network economies, and switching costs, because volume, users, and repeated customer setup begin to compound as demand runs.
Process power and branding, because embedded routines and trusted meaning usually require repeated performance over time.

reviewCards.front: Why is the progression not a deterministic life cycle?
reviewCards.back: Age does not grant power. The stages only guide which powers are plausible enough to test based on evidence, timing, and remaining windows.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use the progression as a timing filter. Name the current stage, then ask which powers that stage can realistically build before funding a desired but mistimed move.

ifThenPlans.plan: If the market is still forming, then I will test counter-positioning or cornered-resource options before spending heavily on brand.
If demand begins to run, then I will look for scale, network, or switching-cost evidence in volume, users, and repeated behavior.
If the business has years of activity, then I will test process routines and brand trust before chasing an early-stage story.
If an initiative has a sponsor, then I will still place it under origination, take-off, or stability and check whether its window is open.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Write your current business or project stage as origination, take-off, or stability. Under it, list one power that fits the stage and one tempting power that is likely mistimed.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the next planning review, sort initiatives by stage before budget. Cross out one initiative whose window has passed or not yet opened, and redirect the spend to a live power test.
